content.text: zone.js never updated your UI. It patched the browser's async APIs and told Angular that something had happened, and Angular then ran change detection, which is the same code with or without zone.js. Zoneless Angular, the default since v21, replaces that guess with notifications your code already sends, like signals and template listeners, and schedules the pass itself. Calling
by hand is the wrong translation.
A team moves its chat app to zoneless. New messages stop appearing, so the fix that ships is

after every assignment, forty of them across the codebase. The inbox works again. Then two bug reports arrive: the unread badge in the header is stuck, and after a reconnect that replays 200 messages, the tab stutters while the inbox renders 200 times in a row.
The belief: zone.js is what makes Angular update the UI. Without it, Angular can't know when to render, so going zoneless means telling it yourself with
For years the two were taught as one thing. When a third-party callback didn't update the view, the standard answer was
, and the next most popular answer was

. Both suggest that zone.js is the engine and that, without the engine, you push the car yourself. The half-truth is real: in a zoneless app, something has to tell Angular that state changed. But your code already sends those signals, often literally, and Angular schedules the render itself.
zone.js was a trigger, never the detector
zone.js patches the browser's asynchronous APIs: event listeners, timers, promises, network requests. When a task that ran inside Angular's zone finished, Angular ran

for the whole app. zone.js had no idea whether anything had changed, and Angular's zoneless guide puts that first among the reasons to drop it: change detection runs far more often than necessary. The detection itself, walking the component tree and comparing each binding with its last value, was always Angular's own code. The API docs describe the switch in one line: zone.js uses browser events to trigger change detection, and
Angular uses Angular APIs to schedule it instead.
Without zone.js, Angular schedules a pass when its own APIs tell it something changed: a signal read by a template is set, a template or host listener runs,

sets an input, or a dirty view is attached. The API reference adds two more: removing a view and registering a render hook. The first notification schedules one pass for shortly after the current task, and every notification that arrives before it runs joins that same pass. Ten signal writes in one callback cost one render, not ten.
Why detectChanges() is the wrong translation

isn't a notification; it's a check that runs synchronously, right now, on one view and its children. That explains both bug reports. Each replayed message re-rendered the inbox on the spot, 200 renders in one task where one would do. And the header isn't a child of the inbox, so the badge it shows was never checked. The calls also leave the cause in place: state that Angular can't see change, so the next developer who assigns a field and forgets the call brings the bug back. Angular's docs pair
, for views you deliberately check by hand.
